questions.q: A pulsed dye laser (PDL) operating at 595 nm is used to treat a port wine stain (PWS) in a 3-year-old child. The primary chromophore targeted and the principle underlying vessel-selective destruction are:
opts: Melanin; selective photothermolysis based on follicular TRT
Oxyhemoglobin; selective photothermolysis matching pulse duration to vessel TRT (1–10 ms)
Water; ablative photothermolysis vaporising superficial dermis
Deoxyhemoglobin; photochemical oxidation causing vessel thrombosis
questions.exp: PDL 595 nm targets oxyhemoglobin, which has an absorption peak near 577–595 nm. Pulse duration (≤10 ms) is kept shorter than the thermal relaxation time (TRT) of the target vessel, confining thermal damage to ectatic dermal capillaries while sparing surrounding tissue. Early treatment in infancy produces better PWS clearance.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin type A (onabotulinumtoxinA) prevents acetylcholine release by cleaving SNAP-25. Which serotype cleaves VAMP/synaptobrevin instead?
opts: Type A
Type B
Type C
Type E
questions.exp: BoNT-B (and serotypes D, F, G) cleave VAMP/synaptobrevin; BoNT-A and BoNT-E cleave SNAP-25; BoNT-C cleaves syntaxin. All prevent SNARE complex formation, blocking cholinergic neurotransmission. RimabotulinumtoxinB (Myobloc) — the only clinical BoNT-B product — is used for cervical dystonia.

questions.q: A patient presents with bluish-grey discoloration of the infraorbital hollow 3 weeks after HA filler injection. Wood's lamp does NOT accentuate the discoloration. The most appropriate management is:
opts: Warm compresses and massage for 4 weeks
Hyaluronidase injection (10–20 IU per area of filler)
Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064 nm laser targeting dermal pigment
Wait 6–12 months for spontaneous HA degradation
questions.exp: The Tyndall effect (light scattering by superficially placed HA particles) causes bluish discoloration not accentuated under Wood's lamp (unlike melanin). Hyaluronidase dissolves the misplaced HA via β-1,4 glycosidic bond cleavage. Immediate treatment prevents persistent discoloration. Skin test for latex/bee-sting allergy is recommended prior to injection.

questions.q: During a TCA 35% medium-depth peel, a 'white frosting with erythematous (pink) background visible through it' is observed. This pattern of frosting corresponds to penetration reaching the:
opts: Stratum granulosum only
Papillary dermis
Upper reticular dermis
Mid-reticular dermis
questions.exp: TCA frosting classification (Fintsi): Level I (erythema with superficial white streaks) = epidermis; Level II (white frosting with pink erythematous background) = papillary dermis — the endpoint for medium-depth peels targeting fine lines, superficial acne scars, and dyspigmentation; Level III (solid opaque white frosting, no erythema) = upper reticular dermis.

questions.q: During a full-face phenol (Baker-Gordon formula) peel, the patient develops multifocal premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). The most likely mechanism is:
opts: Vagal stimulation from pain and skin manipulation
Direct cardiotoxic effect of systemically absorbed phenol depressing myocardial excitability
Anaphylaxis to croton oil in the Baker-Gordon formula
Lidocaine toxicity from combined topical pre-anaesthesia
questions.exp: Phenol is systemically absorbed through skin and exerts a membrane-stabilising (cardiotoxic) effect on myocytes, lowering the threshold for arrhythmias (PVCs, ventricular tachycardia, fibrillation). Risk is minimised by applying to one cosmetic subunit at a time with ≥15-minute intervals, IV hydration, and continuous ECG monitoring throughout the procedure.

questions.q: A picosecond Nd:YAG laser removes tattoo ink more effectively per session than a nanosecond Q-switched laser primarily because:
opts: Higher average power causes greater thermal coagulation of ink particles
Shorter pulse duration (10⁻¹² s) generates stronger photoacoustic shockwaves, fragmenting ink into smaller pieces
Its wavelength covers a wider chromophore absorption spectrum
Greater tissue penetration depth targets deeper tattoo ink deposits
questions.exp: Picosecond pulses (10⁻¹² s) generate pressure waves far exceeding nanosecond Q-switched lasers (10⁻⁹ s), causing predominantly photomechanical rather than photothermal ink fragmentation into sub-micron particles. These are more efficiently phagocytosed by macrophages, clearing tattoo with fewer sessions and less residual thermal collateral damage.

questions.q: Finasteride 1 mg/day inhibits 5-alpha-reductase type 2 in androgenetic alopecia (AGA). The anatomical compartment with the HIGHEST type 2 isoenzyme expression in scalp hair follicles is:
opts: Sebaceous gland cells
Dermal papilla cells
Outer root sheath keratinocytes
Scalp epidermis
questions.exp: 5α-reductase type 2 is concentrated in dermal papilla cells, where testosterone is locally converted to DHT. DHT binds androgen receptors, shortening anagen and causing follicular miniaturisation. Type 1 isoenzyme predominates in sebaceous glands and liver. Finasteride reduces scalp DHT by ~64–70%; dutasteride (type 1+2 inhibitor) achieves ~85–90%.

questions.q: A male patient with AGA shows no response after 6 months of topical minoxidil 5%. The most likely pharmacogenomic explanation is:
opts: He has female-pattern (Ludwig) alopecia and requires 2% formulation
Low scalp sulfotransferase (SULT1A1) activity preventing conversion to active minoxidil sulfate
Receptor downregulation of ATP-sensitive potassium channels from prolonged exposure
Inadequate follicular penetration due to scalp sebum occlusion
questions.exp: Minoxidil is a prodrug requiring sulfation to minoxidil sulfate by sulfotransferase SULT1A1 in scalp keratinocytes. Approximately 30–40% of patients have low SULT1A1 activity and are pharmacogenomic non-responders. Predictive testing (MKSAT urine test or SULT1A1 genotyping) can identify them. Oral minoxidil bypasses this step via hepatic conversion and may be more effective in these patients.

questions.q: Dutasteride 0.5 mg achieves greater hair count increase than finasteride 1 mg in AGA. The pharmacological basis is:
opts: Superior bioavailability and CNS penetration prolonging receptor binding
Inhibition of both type 1 and type 2 5α-reductase, reducing scalp DHT by ~90% vs ~70% with finasteride
An active metabolite that independently promotes follicular growth via VEGF upregulation
Higher lipophilicity achieving greater concentrations within the follicular unit
questions.exp: Dutasteride inhibits both 5α-reductase isoenzymes, achieving ~90–95% suppression of serum DHT and ~85–90% of scalp DHT, versus finasteride's type 2-only inhibition (64–70% scalp DHT). The ARIA study demonstrated statistically significantly greater hair count with dutasteride 0.5 mg vs finasteride 1 mg. Dutasteride's half-life (~5 weeks) also provides more consistent DHT suppression.

questions.q: The corticosteroid component (fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) in Kligman's triple combination formula for melasma primarily serves to:
opts: Directly inhibit tyrosinase copper cofactor, augmenting hydroquinone's action
Suppress tretinoin-induced retinoid dermatitis and inhibit inflammation-triggered melanocyte stimulation
Accelerate stratum corneum desquamation to remove pigmented corneocytes faster
Enhance transdermal absorption of hydroquinone through keratolytic action
questions.exp: Fluocinolone 0.01% in Kligman's formula suppresses the inflammatory response caused by tretinoin (retinoid dermatitis) and prevents inflammation-mediated upregulation of melanocyte activity. It also has mild direct melanocyte-suppressing properties. Long-term use beyond 8–12 weeks risks cutaneous atrophy, telangiectasia, and steroid rosacea — necessitating intermittent use cycles.

questions.q: For laser hair removal in a patient with Fitzpatrick skin type V (brown-dark skin), the safest and most appropriate laser is:
opts: Ruby laser (694 nm) with long pulse duration
Alexandrite laser (755 nm)
Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm)
Pulsed dye laser (595 nm)
questions.exp: Nd:YAG 1064 nm is preferred for FST IV–VI because longer wavelengths have less epidermal melanin absorption, with deeper penetration to target follicular melanin while sparing the epidermis. Ruby (694 nm) and alexandrite (755 nm) carry increasing epidermal injury risk in dark skin. Active epidermal cooling and conservative fluences are still required with Nd:YAG.

questions.q: Compared to CO₂ laser (10,600 nm), Er:YAG laser (2940 nm) for ablative skin resurfacing:
opts: Has lower water absorption, therefore penetrates more deeply per pulse
Has 12–16× greater water absorption coefficient, producing more precise superficial ablation with significantly less residual thermal damage
Targets collagen rather than water, achieving greater dermal remodelling
Provides superior wrinkle reduction due to its deeper thermal coagulation zone
questions.exp: Er:YAG at 2940 nm (water absorption peak) has a coefficient 12–16× higher than CO₂ at 10,600 nm, causing precise tissue ablation with only 1–4 μm residual thermal damage vs 20–150 μm for CO₂. CO₂ produces greater collagen remodelling and wrinkle reduction at the cost of longer downtime and higher risk of scarring and pigmentary changes. Er:YAG offers faster healing with less morbidity.

questions.q: Fractional photothermolysis (e.g., Fraxel 1550 nm) creates microscopic treatment zones (MTZs) surrounded by untreated tissue. The primary clinical advantage over fully ablative resurfacing is:
opts: Greater tissue penetration per session for superior single-treatment efficacy
Rapid re-epithelialization from untreated tissue at MTZ margins, reducing downtime and complication risk
Complete elimination of post-procedure erythema
Higher total energy delivered per unit area in a single pass
questions.exp: Fractional lasers treat only 15–40% of the skin surface per session. Intact keratinocytes from surrounding untreated columns migrate into MTZs, completing re-epithelialization within 1–3 days (vs 7–14 days for fully ablative). This dramatically reduces infection risk, scarring, prolonged erythema, and PIH while requiring multiple treatments to achieve equivalent cumulative improvement.

questions.q: Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) used therapeutically for androgenetic alopecia should have a platelet concentration of at least:
opts: 1–2× baseline (~200,000/μL) — marginal enrichment is sufficient
4–6× baseline (≥1,000,000/μL) — required for adequate growth factor release
8–10× baseline — higher concentration always produces better results
Platelet count is irrelevant; growth factor content is independent of platelet number
questions.exp: Therapeutic PRP for hair loss requires ≥1,000,000 platelets/μL (4–6× baseline of 150,000–400,000/μL) to ensure sufficient release of PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, and EGF from platelet alpha-granules to stimulate dermal papilla cell proliferation and prolong anagen phase. Below this threshold, bioactive factor concentrations are insufficient for reliable follicular stimulation.

questions.q: Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) devices (630–1100 nm, 1–5 mW/cm²) promote hair growth via photobiomodulation. The key mitochondrial target is:
opts: NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I), increasing electron transport chain velocity
Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), enhancing ATP production and reducing oxidative stress in follicular cells
Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II), upregulating Krebs cycle activity
ATP synthase (Complex V), directly phosphorylating ADP to ATP via photon energy
questions.exp: LLLT's photobiomodulatory effect is mediated through absorption of red/NIR photons by cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial complex IV), which dissociates inhibitory nitric oxide, restores electron transport, increases ATP synthesis, and reduces reactive oxygen species. In follicular cells, increased ATP shifts follicles from telogen to anagen phase. Therapeutic fluence is typically 4–6 J/cm².

questions.q: In Follicular Unit Extraction (FUE) compared to Follicular Unit Transplantation (FUT/strip), the graft transection rate is generally:
opts: Lower in FUE due to direct visualisation of each individual follicular unit
Higher in FUE because follicles are extracted blindly with punches without visualising deep follicle angle and direction
Identical between techniques with modern equipment and experienced surgeons
Irrelevant clinically, as transected grafts retain the same survival rate
questions.exp: FUE transection rates range 5–15% (higher in beginners) versus <2% for expert FUT dissection under stereomicroscopic magnification, because FUE punches are advanced 'blind' without seeing the sub-dermal follicle angle. Transected grafts have significantly lower survival rates. Strategies to reduce FUE transection: pre-scoring, sharp vs. blunt hybrid punches, pre-operative follicle angle assessment, and robotic assistance.

questions.q: Trichoscopy finding MOST SPECIFIC for active alopecia areata (not seen in other alopecias) is:
opts: Yellow dots (follicular ostia with keratinous plugs/oil)
Peripilar brown halos (perifollicular pigmentation)
Exclamation mark hairs (proximal shaft thinner/lighter than distal)
Upright regrowing vellus hairs
questions.exp: Exclamation mark hairs — broken hairs with a thin, hypopigmented proximal shaft (reflecting sudden metabolic arrest of the matrix during active inflammation) and thicker distal end — are pathognomonic for active alopecia areata. Yellow dots (most sensitive, also occur in AGA and scarring alopecias) and black dots (cadaverised hairs) are present but not specific. Peripilar halos are characteristic of AGA.

questions.q: On trichoscopy of the frontal scalp in male androgenetic alopecia (AGA), the hallmark finding indicating follicular miniaturisation is:
opts: Hair diameter variability >20% (anisotrichosis) with peripilar brown halos and increased single-hair units
Exclamation mark hairs with yellow dots and perifollicular scaling
White dots (loss of follicular ostia) with no vellus hairs
Starburst pattern with radial white streaks
questions.exp: AGA trichoscopy: >20% hair diameter variability (anisotrichosis — mix of thick terminal and thin miniaturised vellus hairs in the same area) is the hallmark. Peripilar brown/yellow halos reflect sebaceous hyperactivity around miniaturised follicles. Increased single-hair follicular units (normally 2–3 hairs per unit) reflect progressive miniaturisation. This contrasts with AA, where units retain normal calibre but are sparse.

questions.q: Kojic acid exerts its depigmenting effect by:
opts: Blocking melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes via PAR-2 receptor antagonism
Chelating the copper cofactor at the active site of tyrosinase, inhibiting DOPA oxidation
Photochemical destruction of melanin chromophores under UVA illumination
Competitively inhibiting DOPA decarboxylase, blocking melanin biosynthesis downstream
questions.exp: Kojic acid (produced by Aspergillus and Penicillium spp.) chelates the copper ion at the active site of tyrosinase, preventing hydroxylation of tyrosine and oxidation of DOPA. Used at 1–4% in topical formulations, it synergises with hydroquinone and retinoids. Limitations include contact sensitisation (~2%) and potential ochronosis with prolonged use.

questions.q: The primary mechanism by which glycolic acid (alpha-hydroxy acid, AHA) causes stratum corneum exfoliation at concentrations of 10–30% is:
opts: Direct keratinocyte apoptosis via p53 pathway activation
Protein precipitation identical to TCA, causing visible frosting
Reduction of ionic cohesion between corneocytes by neutralising calcium ions that stabilise corneodesmosomes
Disruption of tight junctions between granular layer keratinocytes via ZO-1 inhibition
questions.exp: At lower concentrations, glycolic acid reduces stratum corneum cohesion by neutralising calcium ions required for corneodesmosomes (desmoglein-linked structures) to maintain corneocyte adhesion. This causes exfoliation without protein precipitation (no frosting). At concentrations ≥50%, protein precipitation and epidermolysis occur. Importantly, pH — not just concentration — determines depth of penetration.

questions.q: Topical tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid) exerts its photorejuvenation effects at the molecular level by:
opts: Binding RAR-α/RXR heterodimers, upregulating procollagen I/III synthesis and downregulating MMP-1 (collagenase) via AP-1 inhibition
Blocking vitamin D receptor competing for the same nuclear response element
Stimulating melanocortin-1 receptor to normalise pigmentation via α-MSH pathway
Directly cross-linking existing collagen fibrils to reduce enzymatic degradation
questions.exp: Tretinoin binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR-α predominantly in skin), forming RAR-RXR heterodimers. These: (1) upregulate procollagen types I and III transcription via RARE; (2) suppress AP-1 transcription factor, reducing MMP-1/collagenase expression; (3) normalise keratinocyte differentiation; (4) inhibit tyrosinase (addressing dyspigmentation). Together, these reverse signs of chronological and photoageing.

questions.q: Before botulinum toxin injection for axillary hyperhidrosis, Minor's starch-iodine test is performed. In areas of active sweating, the result appears as:
opts: White precipitate as iodine binds to sweat chloride ions
Dark blue-black colour due to triiodide-starch complex formation in the presence of eccrine sweat
Yellow-green fluorescence under Wood's lamp due to chromogenic bacteria
Red-brown colour from iodine oxidation by hydrogen peroxide in sweat
questions.exp: Minor's test: povidone-iodine is applied to dry skin, allowed to dry, then corn starch powder is applied. Eccrine sweat dissolves iodine → reacts with starch → dark blue-black triiodide-starch complex marks active sweat areas. The stained zone guides precise intradermal BoNT-A injection placement at 1–2 cm intervals (typically 50 U onabotulinumtoxinA per axilla).

questions.q: Immediately after HA filler injection to the nasolabial fold, the patient develops blanching and a livedo reticularis pattern suggesting intravascular occlusion. Within what time window is hyaluronidase injection STILL clinically effective in preventing skin necrosis?
opts: Only within 15 minutes — beyond this, ischaemic damage is irreversible
Within 1 hour — after that, collateral necrosis cannot be prevented
Up to 24 hours — intervention remains beneficial, though outcomes worsen with delay
Hyaluronidase is ineffective for intra-arterial occlusion; only hyperbaric oxygen helps
questions.exp: While immediate hyaluronidase (within minutes) offers the best outcomes, case evidence supports benefit up to 24 hours for arteriolar HA occlusion, which tolerates ischaemia longer than true arterial occlusion. Protocol: immediate high-dose hyaluronidase (≥150–200 IU per affected area), warm compresses, topical nitropaste, aspirin, and close monitoring. Retinal artery involvement (vision change) requires emergency ophthalmology consultation regardless of timing.

questions.q: Polidocanol (lauromacrogol 400) is used as a sclerosant in varicose vein treatment. Its mechanism of action is:
opts: Osmotic dehydration of endothelial cells causing membrane disruption and fibrosis
Detergent action dissolving lipid bilayers of endothelial cell membranes, causing irreversible cell death and venous fibrosis
Precipitation of intravascular proteins forming a plug that organises into fibrosis
Direct vasoconstriction via α₁-adrenergic agonism causing fibrous obliteration
questions.exp: Polidocanol is a detergent (surfactant) sclerosant that disrupts endothelial cell membranes by dissolving their phospholipid bilayers, causing cell death and subsequent fibrotic obliteration of the vessel lumen. It has a favourable safety profile with low thrombogenicity and low allergenicity. Osmotic agents (hypertonic saline/glucose) act differently via osmotic cellular dehydration.

questions.q: Salicylic acid (beta-hydroxy acid) is preferred over glycolic acid for acne chemical peels because:
opts: It penetrates more deeply into the dermis, reaching sebaceous glands directly
Its lipophilicity enables follicular penetration into sebum-filled infundibula, with additional anti-inflammatory (prostaglandin inhibition) properties
It directly kills Cutibacterium acnes through bactericidal action at pH 3.5
It achieves greater stratum corneum desquamation per unit time than glycolic acid
questions.exp: Salicylic acid's lipophilicity (beta-hydroxy group one carbon from carboxyl) allows preferential accumulation within sebaceous follicles, dissolving comedone plugs (comedolytic). It also inhibits cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin synthesis, adding anti-inflammatory benefit ideal for inflammatory acne. Standard acne peels use SA 20–30%. Glycolic acid (water-soluble) does not penetrate follicles as effectively.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman experiences diffuse hair shedding 3 months after delivery of her first child. The mechanism is telogen effluvium caused by:
opts: Iron deficiency from intrapartum haemorrhage causing synchronous catagen induction
Estrogen-prolonged anagen during pregnancy followed by synchronous postpartum anagen-to-telogen conversion after estrogen withdrawal
Prolactin elevation during lactation causing direct follicular telogen shift
Progesterone withdrawal at delivery triggering immediate hair matrix apoptosis
questions.exp: During pregnancy, elevated oestrogen prolongs anagen phase, preventing normal follicular shedding — hair appears thicker. Following parturition, oestrogen withdrawal triggers synchronous conversion of retained anagen follicles to telogen. After the telogen latency of ~3 months, diffuse shedding occurs (postpartum telogen effluvium, 2–5 months post-delivery). Recovery is spontaneous within 6–12 months and requires reassurance rather than treatment.

questions.q: For treatment of atrophic (boxcar/rolling) acne scars with microneedling (collagen induction therapy), the appropriate needle penetration depth to stimulate dermal collagen remodelling is:
opts: 0.25–0.5 mm — targets epidermis for surface texture improvement
0.5–1.0 mm — reaches papillary dermis for mild rejuvenation
1.5–2.5 mm — reaches upper-to-mid reticular dermis where fibroblast-mediated neocollagenesis occurs
3.0–3.5 mm — deep reticular dermis for maximum collagen stimulation
questions.exp: Atrophic acne scars require needle depth of 1.5–2.5 mm to reach the reticular dermis where fibroblasts produce type I and III collagen following TGF-β/PDGF stimulation. Superficial depths (0.5 mm) only improve texture. Depths >3 mm risk subcutaneous adipose injury, bruising, and nerve damage. Optimal depth varies by anatomical site: periorbital area 0.5 mm; cheek/forehead scar sites up to 2.5 mm.

questions.q: For laser hair removal in a fair-skinned (FST II) male with thick, coarse black beard hair, the laser providing the best efficacy–penetration balance for targeting deep follicular bulbs is:
opts: Ruby laser (694 nm) — highest melanin absorption
Alexandrite laser (755 nm) — optimal balance of high melanin absorption and adequate depth for dark hair in light skin
Diode laser (810 nm) — deepest penetration of the three short-wavelength lasers
Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm) — reserved for dark skin types
questions.exp: For FST I–III with dark terminal hair, alexandrite 755 nm provides optimal melanin absorption (higher than diode/Nd:YAG) with sufficient dermal penetration to reach follicular bulbs at 2–7 mm depth. Longer pulse durations (30–60 ms) are selected for thick beard hair to match the larger thermal relaxation time of coarse follicles. Nd:YAG is reserved for FST IV–VI due to its lower epidermal melanin competition.

questions.q: Glycolic acid peels require active neutralisation at the clinical endpoint. The neutralising agent and the rationale are:
opts: Ethanol 70% — denatures glycolic acid proteins immediately
Sodium bicarbonate 8–10% solution or water — raises skin pH above 7, stopping the acid reaction
Hydrogen peroxide 3% — oxidises glycolic acid to non-reactive metabolites
No neutralisation needed — the skin's buffering capacity self-terminates the reaction
questions.exp: Unlike TCA (which self-neutralises through protein precipitation — 'frosting' is the clinical endpoint), glycolic acid continues reacting until pH is raised. Sodium bicarbonate 8–10% or copious water is applied to bring pH above 7. Clinical endpoints are erythema with/without oedema, or a predetermined timer (3–5 min for 70% GA). Failure to neutralise risks epidermolysis and scarring.

questions.q: Non-ablative fractional laser (1550 nm Erbium fibre laser) vs. ablative CO₂ fractional laser for photoageing: which statement is CORRECT?
opts: Non-ablative fractional achieves equivalent photorejuvenation per session with significantly less downtime
Non-ablative fractional 1550 nm produces coagulative MTZs without surface ablation, requiring more sessions but with only 1–2 days of swelling vs. 7–10 days for ablative CO₂
Ablative CO₂ fractional treats vascular lesions more effectively because water is the primary chromophore
Non-ablative fractional is contraindicated in Fitzpatrick skin type IV due to risk of permanent depigmentation
questions.exp: Non-ablative fractional 1550 nm creates coagulative MTZs (no surface ablation) by heating dermal water without vaporising the stratum corneum. Downtime is 1–3 days (oedema/erythema). Ablative fractional CO₂ vaporises MTZs through the full epidermis and into dermis — producing greater collagen remodelling per session but requiring 7–14 days recovery. Both are safer in darker skin types than full-field ablative lasers.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman with Fitzpatrick skin type III undergoes a medium-depth chemical peel with Jessner's solution + TCA 35%. The purpose of pre-treating the skin with Jessner's solution is:
opts: To achieve a more superficial peel by diluting TCA penetration
To degrease and partially disrupt the stratum corneum, allowing more uniform and deeper TCA penetration at a lower TCA concentration
To provide antifungal prophylaxis for the post-peel period
To induce Langerhans cell migration, priming the skin for pigment suppression
questions.exp: Jessner's solution (resorcinol 14%, salicylic acid 14%, lactic acid 14% in ethanol) acts as a 'primer' — it degreases skin and creates controlled disruption of the stratum corneum, facilitating uniform penetration of the subsequently applied TCA 35% at a lower, safer concentration than TCA alone would require for medium-depth peeling. This combination achieves predictable papillary dermis penetration with reduced risk of scarring.
